These bales frequently skew toward PP, but contain mixed polyolefins, styrenics, and multilayer fragments with embedded additives and pigments, which weaken mechanical-recycled property profiles and complicate consistent reprocessing. The observed material variability explains why mechanical recycling alone can struggle to deliver stable melt-flow rates, odor/organoleptic profiles, and mechanical properties— and why chemical or dissolution-based upgrading is often needed to achieve higher-value outlets. To mitigate variability within mechanical routes, Cecon et al. (2024) demonstrated that simple, application-based pre-sorting—e.g., separating HDPE by prior process (extrusion blow molding vs. injection molding) and PP by thermoforming vs. injection molding— substantially tightens distributions in physical, molecular, and thermal properties of PCR polyolefins. This result is actionable for operators: when combined with scalable automation (e.g., sensing-guided sortation), the same nominal polymer family can be triaged into application-specific PCR grades that are more predictable on converting lines. A central bottleneck to quality is fast, accurate identification of mixed plastics on moving belts. The UW team, in collaboration with Michigan Technological University, integrated mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy with a convolutional neural network (PlasticNet) and demonstrated near-100% classification accuracy at 100 Hz acquisition under moving-platform conditions designed to mimic industrial environments (Long et al., 2022). The ML architecture leverages spectral features (and, in related work, 2D Gramian angular representations) to improve class separability—even for dark plastics that frequently defeat near-IR sensors deployed in today’s MRFs. Practically, this real-time MIR+CNN pipeline makes it feasible to: (i) separate polymer families for higher-purity mechanical recycling, (ii) route multilayer or contaminated films to STRAP, and (iii) flag streams with legacy additives/pigments for alternative treatment or de-inking/adsorption workflows. While mechanically recycled resins are critical to circularity, multiple studies in this set quantify how thermomechanical history degrades polymer structure—and how smart characterization can “rescue” value by steering materials to the right processing window and application class. Degradation pathways and triage via rheology. The UMass- Amherst team measured shear and extensional rheology of post-consumer HDPE and PP from three streams and benchmarked against virgin “application-specific” controls, showing that rheology provides sufficient differentiation to assign batches to injection molding, blow molding, or thermoforming use cases (Tillinghast et al., 2025). By adding a secondary sorting step based on initial manufacturing method, they achieved remarkably consistent recovery of application-specific material properties, even with heterogeneous inputs. This offers an implementable QA/QC workflow for reclaimers and brand owners: swap an over-simplified melt-flow-rate screen for paired shear–extensional rheology, then route each lot to processes that are tolerant of its elongational viscosity and relaxation spectrum. The UW team performed repeated extrusion of PP and integrated the resulting experimental data with computer-aided engineering (CAE) simulations of injection molding, demonstrating progressive viscosity reductions and shifts in crystallization kinetics with additional thermal histories, yet showing that process windows can be adjusted to maintain viable molding performance (Estela-García et al., 2025; Estela García et al., 2025).
